claims.text: Hardness and strength in high-entropy alloys are primarily governed by the degree of lattice distortion.
Atomic-size mismatch among constituent elements induces lattice distortion.
Lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion through solid-solution strengthening.
X-ray diffraction peak broadening can quantify lattice distortion in these alloys.
Pair-distribution-function analysis can quantify local strain associated with lattice distortion.
Greater atomic-size mismatch increases local lattice distortion.
Local lattice distortion creates a more rugged energy landscape for dislocation movement.
The more rugged dislocation energy landscape increases resistance to plastic deformation.
HEAs with higher atomic-size mismatch will have higher hardness than HEAs with lower mismatch.
HEAs with higher atomic-size mismatch will have higher yield strength than HEAs with lower mismatch.
The increases in hardness and yield strength will be proportional to measured lattice distortion.
HEAs with minimal atomic-size mismatch will have lower hardness and strength.
Low-mismatch HEAs will have hardness and strength comparable to conventional alloys with similar crystal structures.
The proposed governing relationship applies to single-phase FCC or BCC solid-solution HEAs.
The proposed relationship does not apply to multiphase HEAs or alloys with significant precipitation or ordering.
Electronic effects and stacking-fault energy may alter the magnitude of strengthening.
The hypothesis does not account for grain-size effects or processing-induced defects.

contradictions.description: The intervention proposes changing the selected alloying elements while keeping the overall composition constant. Element substitution necessarily changes chemical composition unless 'composition' is intended to mean only equal elemental fractions; that intended constraint is not stated clearly.
